A Geometric Sieve of Eratosthenes

Number TheoryDivisibilityAlgorithms
Game: Watch a simple copying rule mark dots in a triangle, and see the rows that stay empty: their numbers are the primes.
How to play: Press Clear, then One step again and again. Click a dot to see which dots it is related to, or click between dots to see a step's triangle.

picked dotsiblingsdescendantsancestors

Look for the math

Start with a triangle of dots whose two edges are marked. Take row 2, turn it 60° about its left end and about its right end: the row and its two turned copies make an upside-down triangle, and the dots under the two legs take on the row's marks. Do the same with row 3, row 4, and so on. When it is over, the rows left with nothing marked inside are rows 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, …: the primes. The picture is a version of the sieve of Eratosthenes, from a video by Javier Torres Suárez.

Coordinates for the dots

Call the dot in row r at place k (both counted from 0) (r, k). Turning row r about its left end sends (r, k) to L(r, k) = (r + k, k), and turning it about its right end sends it to R(r, k) = (2r − k, r). Both keep the greatest common divisor: gcd(r + k, k) = gcd(r, k) and gcd(2r − k, r) = gcd(r, k). So a dot only ever passes its mark to dots with the same gcd: its descendants; the dots that pass marks down to it are its ancestors.

Where the marks come from

Going back up with L⁻¹(r, k) = (r − k, k) or R⁻¹(r, k) = (k, 2k − r) keeps the gcd g and always ends at the top: at (0, g) and (g, g), two edge dots, if g > 1; at (2, 1), which is never marked, if g = 1. So a dot inside the triangle ends up marked exactly when gcd(r, k) > 1. In a prime row every inside dot has gcd 1, and the row stays clear. The test checked this on all 5,050 dots of the 100 rows, after comparing every step with the applet's own code.

Siblings and the sieve

Dots in one row with the same gcd d, the dots (r, 0), (r, d), (r, 2d), …, are siblings. Row 12 has four groups, for gcd 2, 3, 4 and 6, and (12, 6) belongs to three of them. Doing the steps for the even rows first, then the rows divisible by 3, then by 5, and so on gives the same final picture; that order is the sieve of Eratosthenes itself.

Two small changes from the applet: it froze when (0, 0) was clicked with “siblings” on, and when the mouse button was let go it left every lit-up dot marked, spoiling the picture. Here the lights stay until the next click and never change the marks.

Tick “ancestors” and click a marked dot, then an unmarked one. Where do their family trees start?
